exercises.prompt: A bottle in the school chemical store has a pictogram showing a **flame over a circle**. What does it warn about?

options.label: The substance catches fire very easily.
options.feedback: Not yet. That is the plain flame pictogram. The circle under the flame changes the meaning.

options.label: The substance is an oxidiser: it can make other things burn far more fiercely.
options.feedback: Yes. An oxidiser may not burn itself, but it feeds a fire, so it must be kept away from things that burn.

options.label: The substance is a gas under pressure.
options.feedback: Not yet. Gases under pressure have their own pictogram: a gas cylinder.

options.label: The substance can explode.
options.feedback: Not yet. Explosives have the exploding-bomb pictogram.

hints: There are two pictograms with a flame. One has nothing under the flame; the other has a circle.
The circle stands for something that does not burn by itself but helps other things burn.
exercises.solution: **It is an oxidiser.** The flame-over-circle pictogram (GHS03) marks substances that release oxygen or otherwise make other materials burn much more fiercely. That is why oxidisers are stored away from flammable substances. The plain flame (GHS02) is for substances that themselves catch fire easily.

exercises.prompt: A can of petrol is kept tightly closed in a cool garden shed. Later, someone opens it next to a lit barbecue. Which statement is correct?

options.label: The hazard and the risk are the same in both places.
options.feedback: Not yet. The petrol is the same, but the situation is very different. Which of the two words depends on the situation?

options.label: The hazard is the same, but the risk is much greater next to the barbecue.
options.feedback: Yes. Petrol always catches fire easily (its hazard); how likely a fire is (the risk) depends on how and where it is used.

options.label: The hazard is greater next to the barbecue, but the risk is the same.
options.feedback: Not yet. The hazard belongs to the substance itself and does not change. It is the chance of harm that changes.

options.label: Petrol in a closed can has no hazard at all.
options.feedback: Not yet. The petrol is just as flammable inside the can. The closed can lowers the risk, not the hazard.

hints: A hazard is what a substance *could* do. Does that change when you move it?
A risk is the chance that harm actually happens in a particular situation.
exercises.solution: **The hazard is the same, but the risk is much greater next to the barbecue.** Petrol's hazard, that it catches fire very easily, belongs to the substance and goes wherever it goes. The risk depends on the situation: sealed, cool and far from flames, a fire is very unlikely; open, with vapour spreading towards a flame, a fire is very likely. Safe practice is all about lowering the risk.

exercises.prompt: Two cleaning products have GHS labels. One has the signal word **Danger**, the other **Warning**. What does this tell you?

options.label: Nothing: the two words mean the same.
options.feedback: Not yet. The GHS uses exactly two signal words, and they mean different things.

options.label: The product marked Danger has the more severe hazard.
options.feedback: Yes. Danger is for the more severe hazards, Warning for the less severe ones.

options.label: The product marked Warning has the more severe hazard.
options.feedback: Not yet. It is the other way round.

options.label: The product marked Warning is completely safe.
options.feedback: Not yet. Warning still means there is a hazard; it is just less severe than one marked Danger.

hints: The GHS has only two signal words. One is for the more severe hazards.
exercises.solution: **Danger** marks the more severe hazards and **Warning** the less severe ones. A label carries only one signal word, the more serious one that applies. Both mean you should read the label and follow its precautions: Warning does not mean safe.

exercises.prompt: During a class practical, a drop of solution splashes into Mei's eye. What should happen **first**?

options.label: She rubs her eye hard to get it out, then carries on.
options.feedback: Not yet. Rubbing can spread the chemical and scratch the eye. And any splash must be reported.

options.label: She rinses the eye with plenty of clean running water at the eyewash, holding it open, while someone tells the teacher.
options.feedback: Yes. Water at once, for a long time (at least 15 minutes), and the teacher told straight away so they can get medical help.

options.label: She puts a drop of a different chemical in her eye to cancel it out.
options.feedback: Not yet. Adding a second chemical can make heat and cause more damage. The rule is to wash the chemical away with water.

options.label: She waits to see whether it starts to hurt.
options.feedback: Not yet. Some chemicals damage the eye before it hurts much. Rinsing must start immediately.

hints: Eyes can be damaged within seconds, so speed matters.
What does the lesson say to use to wash a chemical away, and for how long?
exercises.solution: **Rinse straight away with plenty of clean, gently running water, holding the eye open, for at least 15 minutes, while someone tells the teacher**, who will arrange medical help. Water dilutes the chemical and washes it away; waiting, rubbing, or adding another chemical all make things worse. This is why a laboratory has an eyewash station, and why you should know where it is before you start.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are **safe habits**? Select all that apply.

options.label: Keeping a cleaning product in its original, labelled bottle.
options.feedback: Yes. The label tells everyone what it is and how to handle it.

options.label: Pouring leftover cleaner into an empty juice bottle to save space.
options.feedback: Not yet. Someone, perhaps a small child, may drink from it. Never put chemicals in drink bottles or food containers.

options.label: Washing your hands after practical work, even if you wore gloves.
options.feedback: Yes. Gloves can tear, and chemicals can get onto your wrists.

options.label: Mixing two cleaning products to make a stronger cleaner.
options.feedback: Not yet. Never mix cleaning products: some mixtures give off poisonous gases.

options.label: Wearing eye protection when glassware and chemicals are in use, even for a harmless-looking experiment.
options.feedback: Yes. Splashes come when you least expect them, sometimes from someone else's experiment.

options.label: Eating a snack at the laboratory bench, as long as your hands look clean.
options.feedback: Not yet. Food and drink are never brought into a laboratory, so nothing can end up in the wrong place.

hints: For each one, ask: could this lead to someone swallowing, breathing in or being splashed by a chemical?
Three of the six are safe habits.
exercises.solution:
The safe habits are **(a)** keeping products in their original, labelled containers, **(c)** washing your hands after practical work and **(e)** wearing eye protection.

The others are unsafe: a chemical in a juice bottle can be drunk by mistake; mixing cleaners can release poisonous gases; and food in a laboratory can pick up chemicals from benches and hands.

exercises.prompt: How many numbered sections does a GHS **safety data sheet** have, always in the same order?

feedback.message: Not yet. Nine is the number of hazard pictograms. A safety data sheet has more sections than that.
Not yet. Two is the number of signal words (Danger and Warning).

hints: The sections run from identifying the substance, through hazards, first aid, fire-fighting, spills, storage and protection, to properties, toxicity, environment, disposal, transport, laws and other information.
It is more than 9 and fewer than 20.
exercises.solution: A safety data sheet has **16** sections, always in the same order, so that anyone, anywhere, can find the first-aid advice (section 4) or the fire-fighting advice (section 5) at once. The sections cover identification, hazards, composition, first aid, fire-fighting, accidental release, handling and storage, exposure controls and protective equipment, physical and chemical properties, stability and reactivity, toxicology, ecology, disposal, transport, regulations and other information.

exercises.prompt: A teacher wants to know the first-aid advice and the right protective equipment for a chemical before a class practical. A label has room only for the main facts. Which document, supplied with every hazardous chemical sold to workplaces, gives the full information? (Give its name or its three-letter abbreviation.)

feedback.message: Not yet. The label gives the most important facts, but there is a longer document with sixteen sections.
Close: the teacher writes a risk assessment, but uses another document, supplied by the maker, as the source of information.

hints: It is a sheet of data about safety.
exercises.solution: The **safety data sheet (SDS)**, sometimes called by its older name, material safety data sheet (MSDS). It has sixteen sections, including first-aid measures and the protective equipment to use. Teachers and technicians read the SDS for each chemical before writing a risk assessment for a practical.
